title: The man who saw animalcules: Leeuwenhoek's tiny microscope

body.heading: A draper's side hobby
paragraphs: Leeuwenhoek sold cloth in Delft in the Netherlands, and lenses were tools of his trade — drapers used magnifiers to inspect thread. Curious, he taught himself to grind a single tiny glass bead into a lens of extraordinary quality, mounted it between brass plates, and started looking at everything: lake water, pepper, the plaque from his own teeth.

His microscopes were not the tube-shaped instruments in school labs. Each was a single lens smaller than a fingernail paring, yet the best magnified around 270 times — better than the compound microscopes of professional scientists, whose stacked lenses blurred as much as they revealed. He made hundreds of them and kept his lens-making method secret for the rest of his life.

body.heading: A world in a drop of water
paragraphs: In 1676 he reported 'animalcules' — little animals — swarming in water: what we now call bacteria and other microbes. The Royal Society in London, initially sceptical that a cloth merchant had out-seen every university, sent observers to verify. The animalcules were real, and with them an entire kingdom of life entered human knowledge.

He went on to describe red blood cells, sperm cells and the banded structure of muscle, all with a bead of glass and patience. The lesson of Leeuwenhoek is not the instrument; it is that the biggest discoveries of his century were made by an amateur looking carefully at ordinary things.

takeaway: Cloth merchant Antonie van Leeuwenhoek ground single tiny lenses better than any university's microscopes and, in 1676, revealed microbes — 'animalcules' — living in a drop of water.
